name: Ring modulator
subtitle: PAiA CA-9-style (Craig Anderton, Electronic Projects for Musicians) · Frequency · Effect · Normal

keyIdea.eli5: Multiply two signals and both originals vanish. You get their sum and difference instead, like two notes 'fighting' and leaving new notes behind.
keyIdea.detail: A 440 Hz guitar note times a 100 Hz carrier leaves 340 Hz and 540 Hz. Those don't fit a musical scale, so it sounds bell-like and robotic.

summary: Guitar times a carrier oscillator. The Frequency knob moves the carrier; Effect and Normal blend the wet and dry.

top.label: +V
top.eli5: Red is the + side of the battery: every chip drinks from it.

bottom.label: 0 V (ground)
bottom.eli5: Blue is the battery's − side, and here it is also ground: the 0 V floor.

source.label: Effects Database: PAiA CA-9 Craig Anderton's Ring Modulator

notes: The controls (Frequency, Effect, Normal) come from the Effects Database entry. I couldn't load the CA-9 schematic, so the exact multiplier circuit is unverified. Blocks and board here follow the generic balanced-modulator layout.
Try the test tone at 110 Hz with the carrier near 110 Hz: the difference tone drops toward 0 Hz and you hear a slow beating.

job.eli5: A polite listener: it copies the guitar without pulling on it, and hands a strong copy to both paths.

wire.eli5: A strong copy of the guitar. It splits here: one copy to the multiplier, one to the Normal knob.

job.eli5: Makes the second signal you multiply by. Its pitch decides where the new bell-like tones land.

wire.eli5: A steady tone (the carrier), heading to the multiplier's second input.

job.eli5: Multiplies guitar × carrier, so only new 'sum and difference' tones come out.

wire.eli5: The ring-mod sound: new tones, with both originals gone.

job.eli5: Blends the ring sound (Effect) with the plain guitar (Normal) side by side, then sends it out.

wire.eli5: Your blend of wet and dry, out to the amp.

job.eli5: A polite listener: it copies the guitar without pulling on the pickup.

order.eli5: First, so neither the multiplier nor the dry path pulls on the pickup.

breaks.eli5: The multiplier loads the pickup: duller, quieter, noisier.

chip.note: The original CA-9 used an RC4739 (and PAiA's kit a 5532); Craig Anderton lists the TL072 as a fine modern swap.

job.eli5: A steady humming tone: the thing the guitar gets multiplied by.

order.eli5: It feeds the multiplier's second input and never sits in the guitar's path.

breaks.eli5: Nothing to multiply by, so the effect goes silent.

chip.note: PAiA's tech notes list IC2 as a 565 phase-locked loop. My reading: its VCO is the carrier and its balanced phase detector is the multiplier, one chip doing both jobs. This sketch draws two placeholder chips, so pins aren't mapped to the board.

job.detail: It is part of the oscillator's timing: resistance and a capacitor set the speed.

breaks.eli5: The carrier is stuck at one pitch.

tune.higher: Bigger Frequency pot: the carrier can sweep lower.
tune.lower: Smaller: the lowest carrier is higher, so it stays bell-like.
tune.tooFar: Very big and most of the knob lives in rumble territory.

lugs.eli5: A pot is a resistor with a slider: two end lugs and a wiper in the middle that rides along the track.
lugs.detail: Use all three lugs and it is a voltage divider (a volume knob). Use one end and the wiper and it is a variable resistor (a faucet).
lugs.standard: Standard part: a potentiometer (A = log taper for volume, B = linear).

job.detail: 'Balanced' means that with no guitar playing, the carrier cancels itself out.

chip.note: PAiA's tech notes list IC2 as a 565 phase-locked loop; its double-balanced phase detector multiplies the guitar by the carrier. This sketch draws a placeholder chip, so pins aren't mapped to the board.

job.eli5: A fine-tuning screw that makes the carrier cancel perfectly when you're not playing.

breaks.eli5: A constant whine of the carrier leaks into the output even when the guitar is silent.

tune.higher: Bigger: a coarser null; harder to land the exact balance point.
tune.tooFar: Off balance and the carrier whistles through even with nothing playing.

job.eli5: A mixing bowl that adds wet and dry without them pushing on each other.
job.detail: Its minus input is held steady (a 'virtual ground'), so each input resistor adds its share independently.

order.eli5: Last: it combines the two paths.

honestyNote.eli5: The multiplier is modeled as exact math, which is the ideal a real chip aims for. The dry path really is parallel in the audio model too.

honesty.eli5: Modeled as a Web Audio sine. The real CA-9 carrier waveform is unverified (likely triangle or square).
Modeled as true multiplication, which is the ideal. A real multiplier chip leaks a little and adds some distortion; the trim adds leak back in.
